The government initially downplayed the extent, but the “Comeleak” incident revived memories of a 2016 breach when the entire voter database was leaked.

They claimed to have enough to “map the full election infrastructure”. This breach, coming just months before national elections, highlighted the high stakes of election cybersecurity. It pressured officials to audit and fortify systems (and led to some denying that machine PINs were valid to reassure the public).

Attackers fooled Mailchimp support staff to gain access to ~100 client accounts, specifically targeting crypto companies. Notably, they accessed the mailing list of Trezor (a hardware crypto wallet) and sent all its users a fake “security update” email that was actually a phishing link. Some users entered their recovery seeds on the fake site, leading to their crypto wallets being emptied.

With those tools, they exported client email lists. This is an example of “hack the helper” – instead of hacking Trezor directly, they hacked its email provider. Mailchimp acknowledged the breach and improved its security, but the incident shows how a third-party service breach can cascade into a highly targeted phishing campaign.

Harms include 'breach_of_confidentiality' from access to email lists and recovery seeds, 'insecurity' due to emptied crypto wallets, and 'disclosure' of email addresses to attackers. The emptying of crypto wallets for some users represents a catastrophic financial loss, hence a harm score of 5.

Fraudsters set up fake accounts to pose as legitimate small businesses and bought extensive consumer reports from ChoicePoint. Data included names, addresses, Social Security numbers, credit reports and more. At least 700 cases of identity theft (financial fraud, etc.) were traced to this lapse. The scandal spurred the first U.S. data breach notification laws.

ChoicePoint had even earlier incidents (in 2002) but hadn’t notified victims, showing a pattern of minimal transparency.

The breach catalyzed legislation to mandate better protection of veterans’ data and spurred government-wide security reforms (e.g., encrypting sensitive data on laptops).

The unencrypted discs were sent via ordinary mail and never arrived. This colossal blunder put millions at risk of identity fraud and rocked public confidence in government data handling.

The package wasn’t registered and vanished. Critically, HMRC included sensitive bank and personal data that the Audit Office hadn’t even requested. The fallout included the resignation of the HMRC chairman and urgent reforms: encryption of citizen data in transit, stricter access controls, and a rethink of the upcoming national ID card plans (this breach “nailed the coffin” for public support of a central ID database).

description: In Nov 2007, Facebook launched “Beacon,” an ad system that automatically broadcast users’ outside activities to their Facebook friends (e.g. purchases on partner sites) without clear consent. For example, buying a product on Overstock.com could post an update on your Facebook feed. Users and privacy advocates erupted when surprise messages (“[User] bought X!”) spoiled gifts and revealed sensitive info. Over 50 million Facebook users were affected by default until Beacon was modified. The backlash was one of the first major privacy scandals Facebook faced.

Many didn’t know it was happening – an essential failure to obtain informed consent. MoveOn.org and 50k users protested in a “Stop Invading My Privacy” group. Within a week, Facebook backed down: Zuckerberg apologized and allowed a per-site opt-out (later Beacon was shut down entirely in Sept 2009, and Facebook settled a class-action lawsuit). This episode highlighted how even non-breach privacy harms can damage trust and led to today’s norms around clearer app permissions.

'Deceptive_practices' applies because the system automatically broadcast data without users' clear knowledge, effectively misleading them about their privacy settings. Harms include 'disclosure' and 'exposure' because users' private activities (purchases) were automatically broadcast to their friends without consent, 'intrusion' due to the uninvited sharing of personal information, and 'secondary_use' because data collected for one purpose (purchase) was repurposed for social broadcasting/advertising without consent. This meant that a user’s most-emailed contacts could be exposed on their public Buzz profile without clear permission – e.g. journalists’ confidential sources or an individual’s doctor/lawyer could be revealed as top contacts. The FTC later found Google deceived users and violated privacy promises. In Mar 2011, Google settled with the FTC, agreeing to 20 years of independent privacy audits – the first such penalty on a major tech company. Buzz was shut down in late 2011.
